items.question: Why do you think generating a scene with several people might be too much to ask of a single image-generation model?
items.object: The demands placed on a single image-generation model
items.answer: Maybe we are also asking a single model to solve too many difficult problems at once. Think about what happens when you generate a scene with several people. Now the model has to understand the problem that I'm asking it to model, and then decide how many people should appear, determine where they should be placed, like the composition of the scene, reason about their interactions, because if there's a person, if there's another person, most likely there is some connection. Preserve the identity of the person—we can give, okay, this is my daughter, this is my son, and I want them to be in the picture, not like any random person—and finally render everything together in a single process. So maybe this is too much.
quotes: Maybe we are also asking a single model to solve too many difficult problems at once.

Think about what happens when you generate a scene with several people. Now the model has to understand the problem that I'm asking it to model, and then decide how many people should appear, determine where they should be placed, like the composition of the scene, reason about their interactions, because if there's a person, if there's another person, most likely there is some connection.

Preserve the identity of the person—we can give, okay, this is my daughter, this is my son, and I want them to be in the picture, not like any random person—and finally render everything together in a single process. So maybe this is too much.

The response identifies relationships between the depicted people as something a multi-person scene generator must reason about.
The response distinguishes preserving the identities of specified people from generating arbitrary people in a scene.

items.question: Where do you see the remaining research challenges in text-to-image generation, given how realistic the images have become?
items.object: Remaining challenges in text-to-image generation
items.answer: T2I models, these text-to-image generation models or image-to-image generation models, have become incredibly good at producing very realistic images. The lighting looks natural, the details look right, and the overall quality can be amazing. As with many things we do, there's initial excitement, there's great work coming up, but still, if you look into that, dive deeper, you realize there are many things still to be accomplished. One was controllability: generating multiple people in the same image. People look almost identical; faces kind of blend together. And also, we showed in the past we can run such models on users' devices. You do not need to rely on a cloud service provider. I think most of the models still are limited to 1K by 1K resolution, but then you want to go beyond that. That is a challenge which has not actually been addressed before.

The lighting looks natural, the details look right, and the overall quality can be amazing. As with many things we do, there's initial excitement, there's great work coming up, but still, if you look into that, dive deeper, you realize there are many things still to be accomplished.

items.object: The goals of research on generative image models

items.question: How do you approach the problem of text-to-image models generating nearly identical faces through DISCO?
items.object: DISCO's approach to identity diversity in text-to-image generation
items.answer: When we look at T2I models, our own models also, what was interesting is that this is not an image quality problem. The problem that I mentioned before, like, we are asking the model to generate faces and a certain number of faces, and it keeps generating the same faces, almost identical faces, over and over again. So quality-wise, image-quality-wise, if you look at the pixels and noise and everything, it looks realistic. But the missing piece was that those models, base models, amazing models, had not really learned to create truly distinct identities because existing training objectives focus heavily on realism and matching the user prompt, but they don't explicitly encourage diversity between people, and that is very important. So that observation led us to a simple question: what if identity or facial appearance or any diversity itself becomes an optimization objective? So that led into the idea behind DISCO. Instead of creating a completely new T2I model, we kept the underlying model and fine-tuned it with reinforcement learning. We designed rewards that encourage several things simultaneously. For instance, different people within an image should have distinct identities. You don't want to duplicate, create duplicate faces. That's something we call in the paper intra-image diversity. And across different runs of the same model with similar prompts, same prompt, we should not keep generating the same faces. So this is inter-run, inter-image diversity. So these are explicit new objectives when we train, fine-tune the model. And also, we want the model to generate the correct number of people. If I'm asking to generate two people, that should be two, not three. We are also incorporating that in the objective, and of course we still have the previous image-quality objective there. Putting all together, we use reinforcement learning, something called Group Relative Policy Optimization, GRPO.

items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning helping you make text-to-image models more controllable without requiring a lot of data?
items.object: Reinforcement learning for controllable text-to-image generation
items.answer: We show that you do not need a lot of data. There might be many attributes. Diversity, facial diversity, is one objective; number of people is another one. But then let's say we want to generate a certain action of a person, or pose of the face, or location of the person in the image, or know their body pose and everything. For those, we are saying that you can incorporate such objectives in addition to overall perception or image-quality objectives when we are training such models. But you do not need a lot of data. The key of the paper, for this work, is how to incorporate everything into a reinforcement-learning framework. That would make it possible, and training, fine-tuning such models would also be very affordable. By the way, there is a difference between the quality of the input images going into such models. There is another thing called curriculum learning: starting from simpler scenes and gradually increasing complexity makes learning this reinforcement learning much more stable.

items.answer: One broader lesson from the DISCO paper: sometimes the model seems simply to miss the right objective in training, like the things that I mentioned. And also, it is not mainly an architecture limitation, but how you are providing this objective and training data to the algorithm.

items.question: Why do you think agentic pipelines that select specialized image-generation models will be the ultimate solution for producing top-quality images?
items.object: Agentic orchestration of specialized image-generation models
items.answer: This sounds more like an agentic, orchestrated image-generation framework pipeline, right? Depending on the input prompt, maybe we want to generate, for instance, a realistic scene or a cartoony scene, or maybe there's text or some human-generated graph in the image. For all of it, we have different attributes, like diversity, facial identity. We may have specialized models, specialized processes within those models. So how to pull the right one is something we are working on, such agentic pipelines. Depending on the input, it determines the right tool. If you consider DISCO, one instance of diversity is one instance; the other one is better text generation. So it can go find the right one depending on where you want to apply them and then orchestrate the final generation. I think this is going to be the ultimate solution. One size doesn't fit everyone if you really want to generate something amazing, top of the line. So we need such specialization.

items.question: How do you assess whether DISCO improves diversity in text-to-image generation?
items.object: Evaluating diversity in DISCO's text-to-image generation
items.answer: For this goal, we look into existing benchmarks and then we pull together a new benchmark to specifically help people facilitate further research here and also provide some standardization. We call it Diverse Humans. It's available in the paper. We created this benchmark and evaluated DISCO on that benchmark and also on the other benchmark datasets. We see that when you explicitly impose such a diversity objective, the score—for instance, unique face accuracy detection score—significantly improves. DISCO is around 98, 99, but the models where we started, that don't have such an explicit diversity objective, are very low. There's maybe more than a 10, 20 percentage gap. So this solution that we also talk about in the paper sets a new standard for diversity in text-to-image generation, in addition to human preference score, which is very important. Evaluating the quality of the output is also superior to the base model.

items.question: How do you approach dividing the work of text-to-image generation in your Architect-and-Artist framework?
items.object: Separating planning from rendering in the Architect-and-Artist image-generation framework
items.answer: Instead of asking the model to do everything, we separate planning from rendering, similar to how a human artist would work. So we have two components there. Architect doesn't generate pixels, but instead creates the structure or composition for the scene. Then it decides where, for instance, if there's a person going to be in this image, where it should appear, and if there are multiple people, how they should be arranged, so it should look natural and realistic. Then Artist starts with that composition structure and generates the final photorealistic image, while also preserving identities if we provide an identity. So, yeah, this is a planning-an-architect, then-an-artist type of framework.
quotes: Instead of asking the model to do everything, we separate planning from rendering, similar to how a human artist would work. So we have two components there. Architect doesn't generate pixels, but instead creates the structure or composition for the scene. items.question: How do you think R2's reward function should account for image composition?
items.object: R2's reinforcement learning reward function for image composition
items.answer: We also have this reward function leveraging different objectives that we want to optimize. In DISCO we had intra-image and inter-image, human-perception score, and count accuracy. Here in R2 we also have the composition: can we put the right face into the right place in the composition? That's part of the reward function for GRPO. Also, pose of the face, because now we are composing. We don't want one person to look this way and the other people to look the other way if we're taking a group picture. Those types of things are all combined into the reward function and go into reinforcement learning. Then we optimize that one. The model now learns how to pull all of it, optimize all of it at the same time.

items.question: What distinction do you think is important for understanding how the Architect and Artist models use reinforcement learning to generate images?
items.object: Offline training versus inference in the Architect–Artist image-generation system
items.answer: Architect knows where to position such faces, and Artist, the rendering base model where we started, is now fine-tuned to actually follow the guidance based on the locations coming from the centroid of those face areas. But there are two things to keep in mind. There is a training phase, offline, so these models, Architect and Artist, are optimized to do better. But at inference time, first we take the prompt, and if you want a special person identity to be in that image composition, we provide those images, and Architect generates the locations of the faces. There's no learning there; it just builds on what it learned before. Then Artist, the fine-tuned model, renders it. So this GRPO is on the fine-tuning offline field, and that's an important distinction for sure.

items.question: How do you approach training the Artist image-generation model to render the requested people correctly?

If that is given, then we need to provide those target faces in the training phase. But such faces can be generated, and that's what we did also by another model. These are not necessarily real faces. To automate the training process, the training is very efficient. In training time, those faces are given, the prompt is given, and then the target is generated. items.question: What objectives do you think an image-generation system needs to satisfy when creating a group picture of specific people?
items.object: Objectives for controllable image generation
items.answer: We have to do all of it. We want to make sure that we are still aligned with the input prompt. For instance, if you say three best friends riding unicorns on Mars, like the example in the paper, still we see three people and there are unicorns, and it's Mars. So that is alignment to the input prompts. We still impose that. We also want to make sure that the generated image is high quality. This is human perception score. And there are three people, not two friends. I mentioned three friends, but specific friends, not random people—not many people riding any cross. We actually provide some examples of our faces. We also want our faces to be in the generated picture, so that's the identity-face-matching objective. And another one: we want them to maybe look at the camera if that's a group picture. This is, again, one example of how to improve image generation.

items.question: What do you see as the broader lesson for text-to-image researchers from the DISCO and R2CAMP papers?
items.object: Objective design and task decomposition in text-to-image generation
items.answer: Again, the composition itself would look much more natural because we ask Architect to tell us about the structure of the image. Definitely. But, like I said before, the message is bigger. The message is: hey, community, everyone working on image generation, text-to-image generation models, look what you can also accomplish if you think smartly about the objective function, like the DISCO paper, and also simplify the task, like the R2CAMP paper. Not trying to do everything at once, like, 'I'm gonna generate the composition and the render,' but divide those processes into more manageable parts.

items.question: What were you trying to achieve with PixelRush for high-resolution image generation on smartphones?
items.object: PixelRush's objectives for high-resolution image generation on smartphones
items.answer: Now we ask how to generate images much more efficiently than even what we did before, because Qualcomm proposed and presented many papers at previous CVPRs on how to run such models much more efficiently on mobile phones. But now we are saying: can we push it to the next level? Before, we have been talking about, let's say, 1K resolution, and that's the current sort of limit; even cloud models are kind of limited to that resolution. But the question is now, can we do 4-megapixel image generation, 16-megapixel image generation? The challenge is not only how fast you can run the model. Existing solutions may take anywhere from seconds—50 seconds—to minutes. They're not that fast. But there's a memory challenge also, because when the image resolution gets larger, we need to retain this diffusion process, the latent features, in memory somewhere on the device. So that requires big footprints. How can we run a model such that we generate an extremely large, high-resolution image, and of course the quality has to be high—not just a high-resolution upsampled image, but real details, a lot of details—and it will run in a reasonable time. You don't need to wait like 10 minutes, which is what the current XFR solution requires. And it would run on the memory available on a handheld device like a smartphone. Those were our objectives for PixelRush. We also didn't want to change the existing models significantly, so that is something to note. There are wonderful image-generation models, and we all know some of them by many big companies. We didn't want people to have to find and fine-tune those models. We're saying that you can still use any of those models that you have and follow our pipeline discussed in the paper, so you can use that model and still generate four times, 16 times more pixels.

items.question: How do you approach high-resolution image generation in PixelRush?
items.object: PixelRush's cascade upsampling process
items.answer: It again starts with a prompt, and there is this base generation, like any model. It could be a FLUX model, and then it generates a base image. What I mean by that: let's say a 1K image. Then we have this cascade upsampling stage. That is the part that's new about this paper. This cascade upsample takes this image, which is RGB pixels, not latent space, and then it upscales it—for instance, using any off-the-shelf image-super-resolution solution. It could be bicubic upsampling, or something smarter. It generates a higher-resolution image. So now we have, let's say, a 16-megapixel image, not one megapixel; we have a lot of pixels. Then we take that image and apply an encoder, a VAE, and go into latent space. In that latent space, of course, I mentioned that we are concerned about memory, so we divide that latent space into manageable chunks; we patchify them. Then we improve those latent-space features. We are still in the latent space, and we go through a VAE decoder to the pixel space. Something we need to be very careful of here: there are solutions using patchification, like, 'I'm going to take and create a patch, then another patch, another patch.' When you do that, you create artifacts, visible seams.

This cascade upsample takes this image, which is RGB pixels, not latent space, and then it upscales it—for instance, using any off-the-shelf image-super-resolution solution. It could be bicubic upsampling, or something smarter. It generates a higher-resolution image. So now we have, let's say, a 16-megapixel image, not one megapixel; we have a lot of pixels. We are still in the latent space, and we go through a VAE decoder to the pixel space. Something we need to be very careful of here: there are solutions using patchification, like, 'I'm going to take and create a patch, then another patch, another patch.' When you do that, you create artifacts, visible seams.

The response states that PixelRush partitions the latent representation into manageable patches to limit memory use.
The response warns that creating image patches separately can produce visible seams.

items.question: Why do you favor doing patchification in latent space rather than the original pixel space for image generation?
items.object: Patchification in latent space rather than pixel space
items.answer: For me, there are many reasons. One is latent space is much smaller in dimensionality than the original pixel space. The other one is, in latent space, we can induce noise, and that is a smart way of leveraging noise. That is the other reason.
quotes: There are many reasons. One is latent space is much smaller in dimensionality than the original pixel space. The other one is, in latent space, we can induce noise, and that is a smart way of leveraging noise. That is the other reason.

rubrics.text: The response identifies latent space’s lower dimensionality relative to pixel space as a reason to favor patchification in latent space.
The response identifies the ability to inject noise in latent space as a reason to favor patchification there.

items.question: How do you think about the role of guided semantic noise in the latent refinement stage for high-resolution image generation?
items.object: Guided semantic noise in latent refinement for high-resolution image generation
items.answer: We want some additional flexibility through this injected semantic noise. We want that because we don't want, suddenly, we're generating a big image but there isn't enough texture in the image or high-resolution, semantically meaningful texture in that image. That's why we want the model to have flexibility to add things. We are in the latent space, and then we induce such noise. I mean, we add literally some guided noise into this latent space, because diffusion models—the ones that we are using—do diffusion in the latent space. They start with noise, like random noise, and then iterate it many, many times. I'm talking about the high-level idea of diffusion. Every time it estimates some noise and removes it from the previous noise, and then it clarifies step by step, and ends up with a final image which is noise-free. It looks like a real image. That's how diffusion, denoising diffusion, text-to-image models work. So we're in the same latent space. It's not the pixel RGB, but it's spatially lower. Let's say the input is 1K by 1K; this is maybe 128 by 128. And of course, at every point we have a vector representing the features for that patch corresponding to a pixel. So that is the latent.

items.question: Why did you avoid increasing the latent-space size to generate higher-resolution images?
items.object: Increasing latent-space size for higher-resolution image generation
items.answer: But the memory challenge is there, right? And also it will take forever. The baseline actually does that. They just make the latent space larger, proportional to the target output resolution, which is not what we wanted to do. We wanted to run everything much faster. That's why latent space is much smaller, like the original 1K by 1K in latent space.
quotes: But the memory challenge is there, right? And also it will take forever. The baseline actually does that. They just make the latent space larger, proportional to the target output resolution, which is not what we wanted to do. We wanted to run everything much faster. That's why latent space is much smaller, like the original 1K by 1K in latent space.

rubrics.text: The response identifies increased memory requirements as a reason for avoiding a larger latent space when generating higher-resolution images.
The response identifies slower generation as a reason for avoiding a larger latent space when generating higher-resolution images.
The response states that the baseline scales latent-space size proportionally to the target output resolution.

items.question: How do you approach taking an upsampled image into latent space without making the processing very slow?
items.object: Partitioning an upsampled image before processing it in latent space
items.answer: When we go to latent space, there is a nuance, and it's important. We upsampled the image input, and this is RGB, like a color image. We have a larger version of it. If I go to the latent space of the same proportion size to the target size, it's going to be very slow. So what we do: we partition the input image into original-size patches. Let's say I have a 1K by 1K image. Now I have 4K by 4K on each side, so I divide it into 16 parts. So I have 16 1K by 1K images.
quotes: When we go to latent space, there is a nuance, and it's important. We upsampled the image input, and this is RGB, like a color image. We have a larger version of it. If I go to the latent space of the same proportion size to the target size, it's going to be very slow.

The response describes partitioning the upsampled input image into patches matching the original image’s dimensions for processing into latent space.

items.question: Why do you consider upsampling alone insufficient for super-resolving AI-generated images?
items.object: Upsampling versus meaningful super-resolution
items.answer: We haven't really super-resolved these images in the way that we want, because they are just upsampled, right? We really didn't add any semantically meaningful details. We still have the original prompt, by the way, and that's why we add noise for each latent space.
quotes: These images are not really super-resolved in the way that we want, because they are just upsampled, right? We really didn't add any semantically meaningful details. We still have the original prompt, by the way, and that's why we add noise for each latent space.

The response links adding noise in each latent space to the continued availability of the image’s original generation prompt.

items.question: How do you handle boundary seams when combining independently generated latent-space patches into a higher-quality image?
items.object: Noise injection for blending independently generated latent-space patches
items.answer: In the latent space, we've provided this freedom for the algorithm to generate better, semantically meaningful texture. The algorithm is going to generate a much nicer-looking output image than the input image, given the input image before we went to latent space. But now I have 16 patches, and if I stick them together, arrange them in the original arrangement—they did it independently from each other, because of the memory. Of course, we allow some small overlap, but it's not going to solve it. Those patches are overlapping slightly, but it's not going to solve our problem. So what we also realized is that when we are blending across such latent-space data representations for these 16 patches, we need to do another noise injection when we combine them together. In this case, it's not the same all over the patch in latent space, sampling from the same distribution. We allow the algorithm to generate more noise toward the boundary, but in the center of the patches, maybe less. Now we generate this high-quality latent, which also adds texture but resolves the boundary seam issue.

items.question: Why do you prefer handling artifacts in latent space when generating high-resolution images?
items.object: Latent-space refinement for high-resolution image generation
items.answer: When we generate this high-quality latent, most of the problem is already solved. It will allow, when we go to the VAE decoder and generate this high-resolution image, to be artifact-free. We handle this in the latent space, where it is easier to do, because if we go to the image space, if we start blending in image space, we will most likely blur around the scenes, which is another artifact we don't want.

items.question: What do you think image-inpainting tools need to get right before you would really use them?
items.object: The practical usefulness of image inpainting and InVerField
items.answer: InVerField is not a T2I model. It is an image-inpainting model. So this is image-to-image generative AI. For instance, you can touch an object, create a mask, and then remove that object, or you can bring another object, a new object, into the scene. This is very practical, Sam, because many times we take pictures, but in the background maybe there are things that we want to remove. The challenge is, well, I can still see—you create the texture; sometimes it's meaningful, but then there are those artifacts that you see in the background, like the sand on the beach where you remove the person who didn't need to be in the picture. It's kind of funky looking, and maybe the texture is not really compliant with the rest of the image, or I see literally the artifacts around the boundary. So, yeah, it is like a toy. You can do that, but I'm not going to really use it. But we are saying that you don't need to be there; you can do much better object removal or image inpainting, image editing. That's what this InVerField paper is talking about.

items.question: How do you explain the core idea behind InVerField's ability to produce image edits without boundary artifacts?
items.object: InVerField's use of inverted image noise for seamless inpainting
items.answer: In InVerField, what we do is we have this input image, and we allow generating noise in the background. Then we also have this noise in the mask, like the bird that we want to remove. By noise in the background, I mean the rest of the image. In denoising, we start during training with a noisy image, progressively remove noise, and end up with a clean image. In image generation, we do the same thing: we start with noise and then end up with a clean image. But think about the other process, the way that we actually train those models. When we train, we start with the clean image and then add noise, noise, and at the end it becomes a noisy image. So think about the reverse process, the way that we actually train the model. We can take this input image and map it into noise. So we are progressively inverting a real, clean image into noisy versions. This is very well studied, understood, and it's very fast. In 60 milliseconds, we can take a large image and create a noisy version of it through the reverse denoising process. So this noise is not random noise anymore. It is specific to the input image. If I change the input image, the noise is going to be different. This is about the entire image, and then we have this mask of the bird. Now I add noise there for the bird because I want to allow the algorithm to generate a new bird compliant with my fill prompt, text prompt. So now I change the way that we create this image. But I don't need to change the original model. I can still change the way that I initialize the diffusion in this inpainting. When we do that, when we start with this inverted noise plus the mask and new noise within the mask, first of all, we can retain the background, but we also allow the background to slightly impact the foreground, the mask itself. It allows seamless harmonization and generates high-quality images. But most importantly, there's no boundary artifacts anymore, because we have two noises: random noise and inverted noise within the same image. We're not starting from just noise within the mask.

items.question: Why are you particularly proud of Qualcomm's three video-generation papers at CVPR?
items.object: Qualcomm's three video-generation papers at CVPR
items.answer: I'm very proud of the three video-generation papers because they make video generation accessible to everyone. You can run such models now on your PC, laptop, or phone. Those three papers—I will just mention their names. The first one is Preal Van Van, one of the best open-source, publicly available models. In that paper we're showing, hey, now you can run it much faster—like five times faster—and squeeze it into your memory-limited device. You don't need to run it on the cloud. The other paper is Hybrid Attention, ReHYD. It's a recurrent hybrid attention paper. Again, there's this challenge of where to apply attention, so it does a much better job and makes it faster. And also, attention surgery, because attention takes a lot of compute. These papers are for video generation. Amazing papers.
